canberra.title: Woman, 27, accused of sexually abusing 15-year-old boy
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. A woman has been accused of grooming and repeatedly sexually abusing an unde...
canberra.content:
14 October 2026

The 27-year-old woman hides her face from the media after being granted bail on Wednesday. Photo: Albert McKnight.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

A woman has been accused of grooming and repeatedly sexually abusing an underage teenage boy over several weeks.

It is alleged the 27-year-old Canberra woman, whom Region has chosen not to name for the time being, engaged in multiple sexual acts with the 15-year-old boy between September and October 2026.

The ACT Magistrates Court heard police allegedly found a video of the pair having sex.

The allegations were reported earlier this week before the woman was arrested that same day, an ACT Policing spokesperson said.

She then faced the Magistrates Court on Wednesday afternoon (14 October), charged with four counts of sexual intercourse with a young person and one count of grooming.

“It’s a unique, specific allegation,” her lawyer, Sam Lynch of the Aboriginal Legal Service, said when applying for bail.

He said his client had no criminal history and while she had no home she could go to if she were granted bail, she had several friends she could contact for help.

The prosecutor, who opposed bail, said the matter was complex and the investigation was in its early stages. She said both the 15-year-old boy and the woman were vulnerable.

She also said the woman’s alleged behaviour was extremely disinhibited and not the actions of someone who could be deterred by bail conditions.

Magistrate James Lawton noted the woman reportedly had issues with her mental health and using drugs.

But he ultimately found bail conditions could reduce the risks of her release and granted bail before adjourning the matter to 11 November. No pleas were entered.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: Stadium team aims to include pool and Floriade in plans
canberra.snippet: The architectural team for the proposed city stadium believes the facility will enhance the Commonwealth Park precinct, including the Can...
canberra.content:
Populous architect Al Baxter and Stephen Byron on the proposed stadium site. Photos: Ian Bushnell.

The architectural team for the proposed city stadium believes the facility will enhance the Commonwealth Park precinct, including the Canberra Aquatic Centre and Floriade.

More details have also emerged about the design features the team will explore, including a retractable roof and field.

Canberra Airport has appointed global stadium design firm Populous to develop plans for the proposed covered, all-events 25,000/36,000-seat stadium on Catholic church land at Regatta Place, next to Commonwealth Park.

Airport boss Stephen Byon, Populous senior principal and former Wallaby Al Baxter and members of the Canberra business consortium backing the proposal visited the site on Wednesday (14 October).

Concerns have been raised about what the proposal may mean for the pool, which is meant to replace Canberra Olympic Pool when it closes to make way for the Convention and Entertainment Centre project, and for Commonwealth Park, particularly Floriade.

But Mr Baxter, Canberra-born with a son at the Brumbies, said the project would not be developed in isolation from its surrounds.

Although it was early days, Mr Baxter believed there was enough room on that side of Commonwealth Park to keep the pool.

“There is certainly an opportunity to have a stadium and pool,” he said.

“That has to be tested, but we think that is an exciting opportunity for this site.”

The Archbishop’s House, which the stadium backers hope to acquire.

Airport boss Stephen Byron said the ACT Government was keen to address the pool issue and the team wanted to meet pool users soon.

“Part of that is us working hand in glove with Infrastructure Canberra on this question of the pool. Can it be co-located and Al’s done some work to look at the possibilities of that, and we’ll share that with Infrastructure Canberra,” Mr Byron said.

Mr Byron acknowledged that “a bed or two” of Floriade on the site’s eastern edge would be affected.

“But I think there’s an opportunity for this stadium and all the facilities around it, and if it included the aquatic centre, to really enhance the experience for Floriade,” he said.

Mr Baxter said the stadium could be sited as close as 30 metres to Commonwealth Avenue to maximise the site’s opportunities, and the team would seek a win-win situation where the amenity and access would benefit Floriade and other events in Commonwealth Park.

Mr Byron said the team would not shy away from the challenges and would talk to all stakeholders, including the community, the football codes and concert promoters.

“We’re going to listen to all the problems, we’re going to hear all the concerns, we’re going to analyse them, we’re going to resolve them, and we’re going to find a way to move forward and get this job done,” he said.

Populous designed the Christchurch stadium, which is being used as a reference point for the Canberra proposal. Populous hopes a Canberra stadium can be built for a comparable price of $530 million.

Estimating a realistic cost is in the Populous brief, but Mr Baxter said Canberra, from a construction point of view, was not inherently different from Christchurch and had the advantage of being close to Sydney and Melbourne, where the major infrastructure groups and workforce skills were based.

Canberra also did not have to worry about earthquakes.

Mr Baxter and Mr Byron look at early concept plans for the site.

The team will also look at design features such as a fixed or retractable roof, whether a roof casts shadows, a retractable pitch and the orientation and ventilation to ensure grass can grow.

“As a firm, Populace is really looking forward to working with Steve and the team testing the site, on making sure it fits for Canberra’s unique climate, for the site itself, and for the community,” Mr Baxter said.

He said that while Christchurch was flat, the sloped terrain at this site could be used to advantage to bring people in at upper levels.

The team would also look to maximise existing infrastructure, such as car parks and pedestrian paths.

Mr Byron stressed that the stadium would be an all-weather, all-event facility capable of hosting major concerts, increasing its use and making it more viable.

He said the goal was to put Canberra on the world stage.

“By having a roof and making it an all-weather stadium and having the concerts, you not only change the mathematics and the feasibility from an operation of the stadium point of view, you introduce new revenue streams; you get it to be used more for non-football events,” Mr Byron said. “This is where the economic impact comes.”

Mr Baxter said Kai Tak Stadium in Hong Kong was designed as a sports stadium, but it hosted far more music and cultural events than it did sport.

“We have 60 events a year and only 10 to 15 of those are sporting events and the rest are cultural events,” he said.

“That really drives the use of the stadium, and certainly, we hoped to be able to design something here which would have a similar impact.”

Mr Baxter said boosting the 25,000 capacity to 30,000 for Test matches through temporary seating would also be in the mix.

Mr Byron said the team should deliver design and feasibility studies, including a firm cost, in four to six months for governments to consider.

He said the ACT Government’s response so far had been positive.

canberra.title: PM says he fixed the ATO credit card issue, but Treasurer says he wasn’t rolled
canberra.snippet: Anthony Albanese says he saved the business sector from the ATO’s credit card decision, but Jim Chalmers insists he is the real hero. It ...
canberra.content:
Anthony Albanese at ACCI’s 2026 Gala Dinner. The Prime Minister said he personally intervened after ACCI boss Andrew McKellar contacted him. Photo: ACCI.

Anthony Albanese says he saved the business sector from the ATO’s credit card decision, but Jim Chalmers insists he is the real hero.

It seems the Prime Minister and the Treasurer both want to take credit for dragging the Federal Government to a position the small business community found more palatable after the tax office moved to refuse credit card payments because of the surcharge ban.

A card payment surcharge ban came into effect this month, meaning businesses have to now absorb the cost – or put up their prices.

But when the Australian Taxation Office said it wouldn’t absorb the costs and would instead refuse credit card payments, small businesses said they were given no time to prepare for the change, sparking a massive backlash.

The Treasurer announced on Friday (9 October) that he had asked the ATO to delay the start date for its card refusal.

“Australian small businesses have said the ATO’s announced timeframe was inadequate and we have taken these concerns seriously and acted on them,” Dr Chalmers said.

“The government will provide transitional funding so the ATO can continue accepting credit card transactions until the end of the financial year, with costs to be finalised in MYEFO.

“This will provide more time for the ATO to engage with small business and other taxpayers who currently rely on credit cards, provide more detailed information to those affected, and consult on targeted options to support impacted taxpayers.”

The Opposition described the announcement as an embarrassing backflip, adding that the PM obviously forced the Treasurer’s hand.

Mr Albanese appeared to confirm that theory when he addressed the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s gala dinner on Tuesday night (13 October).

The Prime Minister said he personally intervened after ACCI boss Andrew McKellar contacted him.

“My door is always open. Andrew did text me last Thursday morning, and by Friday morning we had an announcement,” the PM said.

“That was an example of a relationship that takes time to develop as well, that trust.”

Mr McKellar used the same event to express his appreciation to the PM for providing business some “vital breathing space” to prepare for the ATO’s changes,

“Prime Minister, to your credit, your door was open, you engaged, you listened,” Mr McKellar said.

“We welcome that response and we will use the additional time to work with the tax office now to find a sustainable, long-term solution.”

The whole exchange urged journalists on Wednesday morning to ask the Treasurer if the PM had rolled him.

Dr Chalmers dismissed the suggestion, saying he was “not at all” overruled by Mr Albanese, and stressed he was very much himself at the forefront of coming to the aid of the business sector.

“The Prime Minister and I were in discussions on Wednesday of last week,” Dr Chalmers said.

“He had a view and I agree with it, that we needed to provide this longer transition period, to allow the ATO the time.

“We had the same view … We engaged with the business community on the Thursday, as we do frequently, on these sorts of issues.

“Then [Assistant Treasurer] Daniel Mulino and I took a proposal to ministers on the Friday morning after.

“I discussed with the tax commissioner very early on Friday morning, and by late Friday morning, we had stepped in to provide a much longer transition period, so the ATO has the time to consult with business and to get this important change right.”

The Coalition has continued to mock Dr Chalmers over how it played out.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the PM had a “fetish for humiliating his Treasurer”, and it was obvious what happened with the ATO.

“I see this as a consistent pattern of behaviour where the Prime Minister constantly goes in, overrides his Treasurer, humiliates him in public,” Mr Wilson said.

“So yes, I suspect it’s going to sour the relationship somewhat.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor used Question Time on Wednesday to ask the Prime Minister how much humiliation he will put the Treasurer through before he sacks him.

Mr Albanese said the “whole premise” of the question was “completely wrong” because he and the Treasurer were on the same page over what needed to be done for small business.

“The Treasurer and I had a discussion last week,” the PM said.

The Treasurer and I had a discussion last week. We convened the Expenditure Review Committee, and we unanimously, right across the leadership of the government, agreed that the decision by the ATO needed to have a limited period of pause on the ban.

“[It] needed to be extended so there would be a proper consultation with small business.”

canberra.title: Edge to shut last Canberra childcare centre as 11 closures confirmed nationwide
canberra.snippet: Edge Early Learning will close its last remaining Canberra childcare centre on Wednesday (14 October), leaving families scrambling to fin...
canberra.content:
Edge Early Learning Centre Higgins closed earlier this year. The last Edge centre will close its doors on 14 October. Photo: Region.

Edge Early Learning will close its last remaining Canberra childcare centre on Wednesday (14 October), leaving families scrambling to find alternative care after receiving just two days’ notice.

The permanent closure of Edge Ngunnawal follows months of turmoil surrounding the childcare provider, including complaints and regulatory notices. It comes after the earlier closure of its two other ACT centres, including the one at Higgins.

The centre is among 11 across Australia that will shut after administrators failed to secure buyers, while offers have been received for another 53 centres in Queensland and South Australia.

In an email sent to families at about 9:30 pm on Monday (12 October), administrators confirmed that Wednesday would be the final day of care at Ngunnawal.

“As part of the administration process, the Administrators undertook an urgent sale campaign to assess the viable options available for each of the childcare centres of the Edge Group,” the letter said.

“The Administrators have exhausted all efforts in relation to Edge Ngunnawal, but unfortunately, there were no viable offers presented to purchase the centre.”

The closure follows earlier concerns about the quality of care at Edge centres in Canberra, with Higgins among the facilities that had already shut. It also ends Edge’s operations in the ACT.

Sally Tozer, whose daughter has attended the Ngunnawal centre for almost two years, said the late-night notification left families with little time to make arrangements.

“That’s pretty late to receive an email like that,” she told Region, noting that some parents may not have seen the message.

Ms Tozer dropped her daughter off at the centre on Wednesday for her final day.

While she has been exploring alternative childcare arrangements, she said the closure brought mixed feelings because of her family’s previous experience with Edge.

“I’m glad they’re closing, to be completely honest,” she said.

Ms Tozer, who previously raised concerns about how her son Mac was treated while he attended Edge, said she remained deeply unhappy with management’s response. However, she added that she really appreciated the care the staff and educators took of her children.

“But the treatment from other management that I received over, you know, the care of my boy, I could not be happier that they are finally closing, and it should have happened sooner.”

She said her family had a possible alternative placement for her daughter through another centre Mac attended, but she was concerned about other families who might not be as fortunate.

“I am so sad for those other parents. Two days’ notice, but you know, this is nothing for me, because I was given two days’ notice when they kicked Mac out, and they completely uprooted my life back then.”

The administrators said staff would be available on Thursday (15 October) for families to collect belongings, but no childcare would be provided.

Families who have paid fees in advance will receive refunds, which administrators expect to process by the end of October.

Three alternative providers have been identified as having some vacancies: Communities at Work Ngunnawal Child Care and Education Centre, Goodstart Early Learning Braddon and Nido Early School Franklin.

Across the wider Edge group, Goodstart Early Learning has entered into a heads of agreement to acquire 31 centres, while another 22 are subject to offers from six other buyers.

Those transactions remain conditional on due diligence, regulatory approvals and other requirements.

Administrator David Johnstone said there had been significant interest in the business, but acknowledged the consequences for families and staff at centres that could not be sold.

“We acknowledge the impact that the closure of the 11 centres will have on staff as well as families and carers who now need to make alternate childcare arrangements,” he said.

“The Edge team will assist families and staff where they can to find alternate care and employment close to their current centre.”

Deputy Chief Minister and Minister for Child Development and Wellbeing Rachel Stephen-Smith said that, given Edge’s history, it’s not surprising this one was deemed not saleable and unviable.

Ms Stephen-Smith urged affected families to use the Federal Government’s Starting Blocks website to find alternative childcare services and examine their quality ratings and regulatory histories.

She said parents should also ask prospective providers about staffing ratios, the number of qualified early childhood teachers and how long centres had operated under consistent management.

“One of the challenges that we have seen with Edge is that they took over centres that were highly rated, and those ratings persisted,” she said.

“My heart goes out to parents who are having to quickly find a new place for their child and for the children whose care is going to be disrupted through that process,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

canberra.title: Coalition to introduce bill to stop government’s ‘fire sale’ of Defence properties
canberra.snippet: The Coalition says it will introduce a bill to the Senate today aimed at stopping the Federal Government from selling off underutilised o...
canberra.content:
Point Cook airfield south-west of Melbourne is recognised as the birthplace of the Royal Australian Air Force, and is home to the RAAF Museum. Photo: ADF.

The Coalition says it will introduce a bill to the Senate today aimed at stopping the Federal Government from selling off underutilised or surplus Australian Defence Force (ADF) sites.

If successful, the bill would give parliament the power to block the sale of what the Coalition describes as strategic and historically significant assets.

Coalition Defence spokesman Senator James Paterson and veterans’ groups have railed against the government’s February announcement that it will wholly or partly divest up to 67 sites around the country.

Key among these are the historic Victoria Barracks in Sydney and Melbourne, HMAS Penguin on Sydney’s Middle Head, and Point Cook in Melbourne’s south-west which is considered the birthplace of the RAAF.

While the list of sites is extensive, some of the more notable ones include RAAF Base Glenbrook in the NSW lower Blue Mountains, Edinburgh Parks in South Australia, the Fairbairn Golf Course in Canberra, Derwent Barracks in Hobart, Defence Site Maribyrnong in Melbourne, Fort Queenscliff in Victoria, and the Leeuwin Barracks in Fremantle.

The sale of the sites was announced in February on the back of the release of the public version of the Defence Estate Audit and the government’s response to the audit.

Described as the most significant reform to the Defence estate ever to ensure it is fit for purpose, the government said the sale will “provide the ADF with the facilities and capabilities it needs to keep Australians safe”.

The independent audit was commissioned following the 2023 Defence Strategic Review, and the process was conducted by Jan Mason and Jim Miller and delivered to government in late 2023. It says its focus included strengthening the resilience of the Defence estate, mechanisms to accelerate delivery of major infrastructure, and options for consolidation of underutilised facilities.

But while many of these sites are surplus to requirements, observers have pointed out that some of them such as Victoria Barracks and Point Cook have such historical significance that they are already subject to heritage orders and therefore could not be developed, and would therefore be of little value to potential investors.

Others such as HMAS Penguin are still operational, although the plan calls for only part of that base to be sold off.

In a statement, Senator Paterson said the bill would require the Minister for Defence to table a statement in parliament justifying why a divestment decision of a defence estate asset was in the national interest.

“Richard Marles is selling off the family silver because his government refuses to adequately fund Defence,” he said. “It is time the parliament intervened and put a stop to this fire sale.

“More than 108,000 Australians have signed a petition to stop Labor’s defence estate fire sale, which has attracted opposition from across the political spectrum.

“Our military heritage belongs to all Australians. It belongs to the ANZACs. It belongs to our veterans alive today. It is not the plaything of a political party.”

Former Labor Minister and environmentalist Peter Garrett labelled the proposed sale “poor politics” and “laziness” at a recent rally near HMAS Penguin.

Speaking to News24 on 12 October, Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil said a lot of the debate had been “ill-informed”, and used the plans for HMAS Penguin as an example.

“HMAS Penguin is not being divested,” he said.

“The Navy Diving Training Centre, the Clearance Centre that’s there is state‑of‑the‑art, it is inherent to that site. This is being kept, the hyperbaric chambers are being kept, because it is operational and integral and it’s difficult to move it.”

But Mr Khalil conceded that some of the unused land on the base would be subdivided and divested.

“I think the partial divestment of HMAS Penguin is on top of the hill, it’s bushland, it is not the operational centre of the base, that is being retained.

“The point I wanted to make … when we made decisions around these sites, some of them are not being used or underused or underutilised, some of them are empty, some of them are vacant,” he added.

“We’re spending maintenance and sustainment dollars, almost $2 billion over the next decade to maintain and sustain some of these sites, and some sites are historically important, and we are protecting history and heritage.”

In May, members of Fairbairn Golf Club which was named as the 2025 Golf NSW Country Golf Club of the Year launched a petition against its selloff.

“The Fairbairn Golf Club is up for divestment by the government. The club has been around since 1953, providing sporting facilities in Canberra initially for the benefit of Defence personnel and since the late 1990s to the public,” the petition read.

“There is no cost to Defence of running this facility, and the community health and social benefits are important. There are currently insufficient golf courses in the ACT to meet demand, and closing the Fairbairn golf course will significantly impact community access to golf courses.

“The course is an important part of the ACT’s sporting, social and recreational infrastructure.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

australia.title: Child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as ‘safe’ day after she was admitted to hospital in coma
australia.snippet: Inquest into death of eight-year-old Queensland girl who was denied insulin by her religious parents told her case was complex Get our br...
australia.content:
A child safety officer incorrectly assessed Elizabeth Struhs as “safe” one day after she arrived at hospital in a coma and nearly died due to the neglect of her parents, a coroner’s court has heard.

A Queensland coronial inquest heard evidence on Wednesday from one of the two child safety officers who ultimately decided to return the then six-year-old, who had type 1 diabetes, to the care of her parents at their home in Toowoomba.

She died there on 7 January 2022 while her parents, Kerrie and Jason, and other members of their small religious sect prayed for her miraculous healing or resurrection.

None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.

The child safety officer was given the duty of investigating Elizabeth’s home after she presented to Toowoomba hospital in a coma suffering from diabetic ketoacidosis on 17 July 2019. He later became her case worker.

Just one day later – after she was transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane – another child safety officer who assisted him completed an initial safety assessment of Elizabeth. She marked her “safe”.

But her colleague told the court on Wednesday that Elizabeth should have been recorded as “unsafe” because they didn’t have enough information about her circumstances at the time.

Elizabeth was later assessed as a child in need of protection, a legal standard under the child safety act.

In 2021, both Jason and Kerrie were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to their daughter as a result of the 2019 incident, and Kerrie was jailed.

The child safety officer later had a conversation with a doctor from the Queensland children’s hospital who told him Elizabeth was lucky not to have died and that Kerrie had not shown remorse as a result of the incident.

The doctor said Kerrie continued to not believe in medicine and that it would be unsafe for her daughter to live with her until she changed her views, the inquest heard.

“The pressure on dad around such strong religious beliefs will be difficult,” the doctor told him, according to his contemporaneous notes presented in court on Wednesday.

“The team feel that the only way to force mum to see the concerns may be for Elizabeth to be out of home.”

Elizabeth was sent home despite the objections of the Brisbane-based specialist paediatric doctors.

The doctor told the court on Monday that she felt “stonewalled” by the officer after raising concerns about Elizabeth’s safety at home.

Elizabeth was ultimately returned home to live with her family, with an intervention parental agreement: a short-term, voluntary arrangement that allows child safety authorities to aid a child in danger without a child protection order, the inquest heard.

On Wednesday, the child safety officer said that the safety plan they adopted for Elizabeth “in hindsight, could have been more robust”.

But he said he didn’t have a clear recollection of a meeting in which they discussed the idea of adopting the plan.

“I do recall being in two minds about the best outcome for Elizabeth and her siblings, specifically Elizabeth being able to remain at home and connected with her family or out of home,” he said in a written statement provided to the court.

He said it was a difficult decision and that there were practical considerations of how to manage the complex case.

The child safety officer said it was significant that Jason had repeatedly committed to provide insulin for his daughter. Elizabeth required daily insulin injections to live.

The inquest previously heard Jason, a longtime sceptic of his wife’s religion, subsequently provided medical attention for Elizabeth for two years. But he ceased doing so after being convinced to convert and then to stop treating her by the members of the group, and he stopped her insulin in late 2021, causing her death.

All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including the group leader, Brendan Stevens.

The inquest continues.

australia.title: Labor’s bill to cut private health insurance rebate blocked by Greens over pensioner carve-out
australia.snippet: Almost 80,000 older Australians expected to end private health cover by 2028-29 as a result of Albanese government’s proposal Get our bre...
australia.content:
Labor’s bid to cut the private health insurance rebate for over-65s has been blocked in parliament, with the Greens insisting they will withhold support unless pensioners receive a carve-out from the new rules.

The proposed changes, which would take effect from April 2027, would save the federal budget $3bn.

It marks another defeat for a key cost-saving measure after the government was forced to back down on its plan to cap allied health payments for veterans which would have saved $748m over three years.

People who are 65 or over currently receive a larger rebate on their premium, with the rebate higher for those 70 and over.

The Greens, Coalition and crossbench senators teamed up in the Senate on Wednesday to block Labor’s bill. In a rare move, the bill was discharged from the upper house, meaning it will need to be reintroduced if Labor tries to push ahead.

The health minister, Mark Butler, said the government planned to reintroduce the same bill to parliament on Thursday.

“It is important that the parliament have a proper debate, that these really important questions for older Australians are not held hostage to political stunts, but instead that the elected members of the House of Representatives and elected senators take these issues seriously and debate them properly,” he said.

Almost 80,000 older Australians are expected to ditch their private health cover by 2028-29 as a result of the Albanese government’s proposal, according to health department modelling released under freedom of information laws.

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said the party would only offer its support for the changes if the government excluded pensioners.

“We say to Labor, if you want to bring this bill back … [by] carving out 1.2 million pensioners from this attack … come and talk to us,” he said.

“We will pass it in a heartbeat. But we will not be joining with Labor to punch down on pensioners in the middle of a cost of living crisis.”

Butler said the new Greens leadership “spied a political opportunity” to team up with the Coalition.

The chief executive of the Council on the Ageing Australia, Patricia Sparrow, rejected the planned savings being linked to aged care funding commitments.

“Older Australians shouldn’t have to choose between protecting their health and paying for everyday essentials. Nor should they be asked to choose between affordable healthcare and a properly funded aged care system,” she said.

The shadow health minister, Anne Ruston, said the policy would have affected up to 1.5 million pensioners.

“The idea that a government would have to cut the health system to need to pay for the aged care system … just reflects the fact of how much this government has lost control of their budget bottom line,” she said.

The proposal has been criticised by the states and territories, which warn their health services will come under increasing pressure.

The Victorian health minister, Ingrid Stitt, said she had raised concerns with Butler, vowing to oppose “any move that makes it harder for Victorians to get the care they need”.

“Any commonwealth savings shouldn’t come at the expense of older Victorians or simply shift pressure on to our public hospitals,” she said.

The New South Wales health minister, Ryan Park, said the state was already experiencing “significant pressure” on its public health system due to the commonwealth’s failure to provide sufficient aged care placements.

“This is not good for [the aged] and they deserve better,” he said.

The Queensland health minister, Tim Nicholls, said the “additional pressure will come at the expense of the thousands of older Australians already stuck in hospitals right across the country”.

The Tasmanian health minister, Bridget Archer, said the federal government was “already refusing to provide solutions to get aged care patients out of hospital and this dog of a policy will make things even worse”.

australia.title: Video recording device found in cabin of HMAS Leeuwin navy ship in Cairns
australia.snippet: Defence announcement comes after Jacqui Lambie tells parliament a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on board Get our br...
australia.content:
A “video recording device” was found in the cabin of a Royal Australian Navy ship in Cairns, the defence department has revealed, just hours after senator Jacqui Lambie alleged in parliament that a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on the vessel.

The department confirmed on Wednesday afternoon that a device had been found aboard the HMAS Leeuwin three days earlier. In a statement after Guardian Australia had contacted the department for response to Lambie’s allegations, a spokesperson said police were investigating, but did not reveal further details about where the device was located.

“On 11 October 2026, Defence became aware that a video recording device had been located in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin, while alongside in Cairns, Queensland,” they said.

“The incident was referred to the Joint Military Police Unit and Defence is working with civilian authorities. Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form.”

On Wednesday morning, Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate that she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.

“The sender told me that concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors’ showers facilities on the vessel HMAS Leeuwin, based in Cairns,” she said in the Senate.

“I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered.

“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask Navy.”

Guardian Australia asked the department if any perpetrator had been identified, if the defence force was aware of hidden cameras being found in other navy facilities, and if any such footage from hidden cameras had been found to have been shared online.

The department did not directly answer those questions. In its statement, it said HMAS Leeuwin had “remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship’s crew”.

“The welfare of individuals remains Defence’s priority, and support is ongoing. As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time,” it said.

Asked at a subsequent press conference about the incident, Lambie said she was unhappy with the department’s response.

“Defence needs to know this. Your people had a gutful, and if there was abuse going on, they’re now coming to me. OK, I’m right on their tail. Enough is enough. Get control of what is going on in the defence force,” she said.

“What I want to know is, have they gone around on the rest of those boats, the subs, whatever, and had a look and make sure there’s no other cameras? Because we are not sure whether it’s coming from contractors that go on them, or whether it’s come from defence members.”

australia.title: Trade minister says Coalition MPs walked out of meeting on EU trade deal – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia missing out on $45bn of revenue from resou...
australia.content:
Key events

    What we learned today, Wednesday 14 October
