What we learned today, Wednesday 14 October

Luca Ittimani

Thanks for joining us today. We’ll close the blog there.

Here were the key events:

  • The Nationals brought pineapples to parliament to warn against “risky” imports at issue in negotiations over a trade deal with the European Union.

  • Labor’s trade minister, Don Farrell, said Coalition MPs walked out of a meeting on the proposed trade deal.

  • The Reserve Bank has warned staff their pay rise “will not proceed” as planned, if it is rejected in a vote that opens tomorrow.

  • The Liberal MP Angie Bell said she reached out to Anne Aly over her “poor choice of words” when suggesting she should be “shamed and stoned”.

  • Pauline Hanson said Bell’s comments were said “in the heat of the moment” and a Nationals MP defended the comments.

  • Australia and Jordan signed a joint statement on defence and security.

  • Angus Taylor claimed the prime minister repeatedly “humiliated” the treasurer.

  • Jim Chalmers introduced Labor’s trusts tax legislation to the House of Representatives.

  • A Coalition bid to send the bill to an inquiry failed but the Greens deputy leader called for an inquiry to close “loopholes” in the tax.

  • Anthony Albanese said his “thoughts and prayers” were with Pope Leo XIV following the pope’s cancer diagnosis.

Krishani Dhanji will be back with you tomorrow for the last sitting day of this week. See you then.

Husic rejects Wong’s criticism of Palestinian Authority delaying elections

Ed Husic has pushed back at Penny Wong’s criticism of the Palestinian Authority delaying its elections until 2027.

The foreign minister, with counterparts in Canada, France and the United Kingdom, has called the delay “deeply disappointing”.

Husic has told the ABC:

Gaza has been levelled. There are Palestinians trying to hold on to their homes in the West Bank. Imagine trying to put a polling station in that circumstance.

The issue is, trying to make sure you have a election process that you can be confident in, that is held in a time that that can occur, and I don’t think it can be, not with those current circumstances …

And there are people who say, well, and the foreign minister I know has made this point, that our [Australia’s] recognition of the state of Palestine was predicated on the elections, and I absolutely agree. But there is a time and a place. And this is not the right time.

Husic says he understands ‘discomfort’ at PM’s office helping write a letter to itself

Ed Husic, the Labor backbencher, has backed independent David Pocock’s concern at the process by which the AI parliamentary committee wrote its letter to the prime minister.

Anthony Albanese’s office signed off on language in the bipartisan letter on the AI inquiry before it was sent to the prime minister. Husic told the ABC:

I think the time for inquiries is over … But having said that, if we are going to do an inquiry, the expectation is it’s done thoroughly. Normally the process would be if you want to do an interim report, you do a report, and the secretariat gets involved, and it puts it together, and the committee has a chance to go through it, and make sure that it’s a thorough response.

So, you know, I can understand why there would be some discomfort about, you know, a letter being put forward in the way that it was done. If you’re going to do it, do it right.

Greens deputy leader hopes to be in government in ‘not too distant future’

The Greens’ new deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May, says she wants the minor party to form government and hopefully soon.

Hodgins-May was on the ABC just now, discussing her objections to the government’s planned reform to its minimum 30% tax rate on discretionary trusts.

She said the Greens still wanted the reforms to happen “this year” but wanted an inquiry to find and close any loopholes in the proposed system:

We’re saying what the government’s dished up at present isn’t good enough. They’ve watered down something to the point where we’re uncomfortable with it. We think that it’s going to create further inequity in the taxation system and benefit the 1% …

Even if it’s not perfect, well, we’re going to fight for it to be better than it is.

Asked whether she accepted that the Greens could not make the laws “perfect,” Hodgins-May said:

Well, until the Greens are in government, which I do hope happens in the not too distant future – when we can put up legislation that we are incredibly proud of and that we think Australians would also get behind – yes, there’s a level of compromise. But let’s be clear, we are sending this to inquiry. We will interrogate it.

US is repeatedly warning Labor on algorithm reforms, says trade minister

Don Farrell has said the US representatives to Australia have repeatedly complained about Labor’s planned algorithm laws but made no direct threats.

The digital duty of care laws are expected to be introduced to parliament this week. Farrell told the ABC:

They’ve been raised with me every time I’ve met with the Americans. We obviously have a difference of opinion. We certainly don’t believe anything we are doing is contrary to our free trade agreement … I’ve tried to explain to the Americans that our objective is to protect our citizens, particularly young people. And so far, there hasn’t been a direct response.

He said the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, has raised a range of social media issues but there had never been a threat of a consequence for the laws.

Farrell added:

In a few minutes, I’m meeting the new American ambassador. He may or he may not [mention the laws]. I don’t know. But if he does, I will explain to him, as I’ve explained to Jamieson Greer, our job as an Australian government is to protect our citizens, and this is one of the ways we’re doing it.

Trade minister says Coalition MPs walked out of meeting on EU trade deal

The trade minister says Coalition representatives have walked out of meetings on the European Union trade deal but some of its members might still be interested in getting the deal done.

Don Farrell has told the ABC that Ted O’Brien had walked out on him while he was explaining the deal, along with the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, who protested the trade deal while holding a pineapple earlier today.

But Farrell told Patricia Karvelas the Coalition’s and Greens’ objections to the deal did not mean it could not proceed, adding:

I have to find nine sensible senators beyond the 30 that I’ve got. I’m discussing it with everybody. And don’t think for one moment, Patricia, that the opposition is united in their position against this agreement …

I’m hopeful, in fact, I’m perhaps even confident that there are enough senators in the Australian Senate right now who understand just how important this agreement is for Australia to get through.

RBA warns staff pay rise ‘will not proceed’ if rejected ahead of vote

The Reserve Bank of Australia has told its staff they will miss out on their pay rise if they don’t support a disputed wage deal.

RBA staff rejected a 9.5% increase over three years in July and have fought management for a better offer but the bank will put a roughly similar offer to a vote tomorrow.

Susan Woods, the RBA’s chief operating officer, told staff in an email today the 9.5% offer was competitive. She said:

We have genuinely negotiated to arrive at this position and are at the limit of what we can responsibly offer while meeting our obligations as a public institution and Australia’s central bank.

Staff have already missed six weeks of pay rise as their deal would have started in September. Woods told staff the RBA would not offer any back pay, adding:

This is the Bank’s best offer for the 2026 EA. A further “no” vote will not recover the salary already forgone, and the proposed 3.7 per cent increase will not proceed … Bargaining would continue, with no guarantee that this would result in a higher wage outcome.

The RBA has compared its bargaining to federal public service, which is offering 9%, and the Commonwealth Bank, which yesterday agreed pay rises over three years of 13% for its lowest paid staff but 5% for those on over $165,000.

The Finance Sector Union has asked RBA staff to reject the deal and fight for an 11% three-year deal. The vote will close at 5pm AEDT on Monday.

Luca Ittimani

Thanks Krishani and hello readers! I’ll be with you for the rest of the afternoon.

Krishani Dhanji

That’s all from me on the politics blog today, thank you for following along.

I’ll leave you with the magnetic Luca Ittimani (to borrow from Jason Clare) for the rest of the afternoon, and will see you back here bright and early tomorrow!

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • Anthony Albanese said he and Jim Chalmers were in complete lockstep on delaying the ATO credit card ban, trying hard to pour cold water over commentary that the prime minister had gone over his treasurer’s head. Angus Taylor said Chalmers’ had been “humiliated” and called for him to be sacked.

  • Small business minister Anne Aly faced more questions from the opposition who accused her of “waging a war” on small business. She tried to counter saying small business numbers were going up.

  • Communications minister Anika Wells used a dixer to implore the Coalition to support the government’s digital duty of care bill.

  • Josh Frydenberg’s name got more of a workout by Labor - it’s getting old so here’s to hoping that soon ends.

  • And despite an at times pretty rowdy question time, as well as a few behavioural warnings, there were no ejections today!

Penry Buckley

NSW One Nation leader tours state parliament, says party is ‘living rent free’ in government’s head

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, has been a surprise presence in and around state parliament today, appearing in the upper and lower house and hosting an unannounced press conference outside.

The NSW party does not have any MPs in either chamber, but is polling at 25%, in second place behind Labor, according to a September Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll. During question time in the legislative assembly, Newman stood just inside the doorway by the opposition benches. He was asked to leave by the serjeant at arms before the premier, Chris Minns, used a question to criticise Newman for rejecting a legislative bid to compel One Nation to cost their election promises.

Newman, the candidate for the lower house seat of Cessnock at next year’s election, told reporters this afternoon that One Nation was “living rent free in their heads”. “No seats in upper or lower house, they still have to mention us,” he said.

Newman was accompanied at a press conference by Libertarian upper house member, John Ruddick, who, like him, was also wearing a bright orange tie. Asked if Ruddick was joining One Nation, Newman, who later insisted he was not on a “recruitment drive”, said:

We haven’t had that discussion at all. John’s John, I’m me. Don’t let the orange tie fool you.

Newman, a former investment banker and trade bureaucrat, is not a Cessnock local and returned to Australia after spending 25 years working in Japan. He was quizzed on his knowledge of the electorate, fielding questions on his favourite Cessnock pub, restaurant, what he likes to order there and the name of the local footy team.

The assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, gets the final dixer, and tries to get in a few last jabs to the Coalition on Josh Frydenberg.

One of the jokes take a couple of goes to land.

After that the PM mercifully calls time on QT.

Just one more to go for the week.

Nationals deputy leader Darren Chester asks the prime minister if he takes responsibility “for the average mortgage–holder now paying $30,000 more per year because of the 16 interest rate rises under his government.

Anthony Albanese says he does take responsibility for the two budget surpluses and budget improvements under the Labor government.

The fact that we’ve produced eight separate either budgets or budget updates – every one of which has had a savings measure in it. We take responsibility for the fact that over 260,000 Australians...

The opposition tries to interject – the PM hasn’t said he takes responsibility for the higher mortgage payments, and the Coalition are trying to back him into a corner.

It doesn’t work, Albanese opts to sit down, indicating he’s finished his answer.

Sharkie questions government over aged care funding

Independent Rebekha Sharkie is next and asks the aged care minister why the Australian National Aged Care Classification – the funding model for residential aged care – has only received a 2.55% funding increase, below inflation.

She asks:

We need 10,000 new aged care beds annually, last year just 800 were added. Thousands of our elderly are stuck in hospitals waiting for an aged care bed around our nation. Minister, this is a disaster on your watch. Will you lift the ANACC funding to at least match inflation?

The aged care minister, Sam Rae, says the government increases funding to the ANACC based on independent advice.

The government sets aged care funding based on the independent advice from the independent funding authority. It provides expert [advice] to myself and Minister Butler … with a view to working out the efficient cost of delivering care.

‘Miscommunication’ over digital duty of care, Wells tells One Nation MP

Anika Wells gets another question on the DDOC, this time from One Nation’s David Farley, who asks about an issue which has strongly activated right-wing opponents of the bill – powers for regulators to establish “sockpuppet” accounts online.

Wells said such fake accounts had been used by “malevolent” actors online for nefarious purposes, but that regulators would use it for “mystery shopping” purposes, like doing research on how platforms serve up particular types of content to particular types of users.

They need to mystery shop what is happening on platforms in order to test whether the platforms are actually doing what they say that they are doing. So if they say they are asking a 14-year-old for their age, we need to test if they are actually doing that.

What the eSafety commission, or accredited researchers do, is create an account, as a 14-year-old girl, and test those hypotheses. They do it for good purposes.

We think that we should be able to mark tech platforms’ homework – they should not get to mark their own homework. So that is the purpose of sockpuppets.

Prime minister quiet on goldmine court case

Nationals MP Jamie Chaffey asks the prime minister about the federal court ruling that the government blocked a billion-dollar goldmine in central-west NSW without authority.

Anthony Albanese doesn’t want to bite – he says it’s a legal matter so won’t comment.

I understand the federal court found the declaration was not validly made. This was a complex legal case and as it’s a legal matter we will work through the judgment together with the attorney general and we’ll consider the findings very carefully indeed.

‘Magnificent, marvellous, magnetic’, the House plays a guessing game on Clare’s dixers

There’s a bit of a running joke on the education minister, Jason Clare’s, dixers.

Clare loves a bit of alliteration when thanking a backbencher for a pre-planned softball question.

Yesterday it was the “dazzling member for Deakin”.

Today the question comes from the member for Menzies, Gabriel Ng, and the opposition tries to guess the adjective as Clare steps up to the dispatch box.

They try, “magnificent”, and “marvellous”.

Clare laughs and thanks “the magnetic member for Menzies”.

‘Put your politics to the side’, Wells urges Coalition on online safety

Josh Butler

The communications minister, Anika Wells, says Labor’s proposed digital duty of care “moves the safety net upstream” to require tech companies do better, taking a shot at the Coalition for refusing to discuss the legislation.

Wells will introduce the legislation tomorrow, then give a major speech at the National Press Club about it. She tells question time Australia already has “one of the most comprehensive online safety frameworks in the world”, but more work is needed.

“An independent statutory review has found that it is not able to cope with the growing scale of problems in the online world. Just last week, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, warned that the police cannot be the only safety net when it comes to the radicalisation of young people online. By the time the AFP is knocking on a door, the harm is already done.

She said the digital duty of care would “shift the burden from the shoulders of victims … to the companies that are creating the environments where harms occur.”

It moves the safety net upstream to the people who design the product before it ever reaches the child.

Wells said she was surprised at the Coalition’s reticence over the bill, after shadow spokesperson Sarah Henderson said the opposition wasn’t interested in negotiating.

Last week, they were criticising our online safety laws for not having enough parliamentary scrutiny. This week, they’re criticising our online safety lords for having too much parliamentary scrutiny.

Put your politics to the side, listen to the AFP commissioner, and help us pass these laws.

Independent Monique Ryan is next and asks the health minister if he can guarantee that Victorian children won’t slip through the gap under Thriving Kids – which will replace NDIS services for children under nine with low level needs.

Mark Butler says that the state delivery of the program basically mean that those jurisdictions provide some of the services they used to before the NDIS was implemented.

He concedes there will be a degree of variation between jurisdictions about the type of service and the location of that service.

But he says there will still be standards they will have to meet:

We have been very clear that there are outcomes that we expect to see, performance indicators that we expect to have met by all state and territory jurisdictions. They are incorporated into the Thriving Kids bilateral agreements that all state governments have signed.

australia.title: Decoding America: Everything you need to know about the midterms – video
australia.snippet: In this episode of Guardian Australia’s US politics podcast, co-hosts Reged Ahmad and Jonathan Yerushalmy take a look at the midterms, wh...
australia.content:
In this episode of Guardian Australia’s US politics podcast, co-hosts Reged Ahmad and Jonathan Yerushalmy take a look at the midterms, which are coming up in early November. All 435 house seats are up in this election as representatives only serve fixed two-year terms. In the Senate, 35 of 100 seats are up for grabs too, as senators serve six-year terms.

There are many predictions of a blue wave – a big win for the Democrats, who are tipped to take back the House and Senate. But are pollsters being too optimistic? What are the factors that could instead allow the Republican party and the Trump administration to hold onto power in Congress? They also look at why the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, has been ousted from her job – and whether criticism of the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, is fair

  • Abdul El-Sayed: Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial

  • Federal judge orders temporary halt to taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads

world.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
world.snippet: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approve...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.

But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year. Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.”

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.

Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neo-colonialist” and “damaging”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”

It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.

The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.

Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “cancelled or suspended.”

Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported by Rolling Stone. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

  • This article was amended on 13 October 2026. A previous version said CIDRAP first reported news that the research trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee. Rolling Stone had actually reported the news first.

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

world.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
world.snippet: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the f...
world.content:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

world.title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
world.snippet: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood Egyptian journalists...
world.content:
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”
